Missing pairs then fail during composition rather than halfway through an effectful operation. The check is complete for `R`; it covers the application only if `R` covers its reachable uses. Guard calls outside that scope. Loading another extension requires constructing or qualifying another composition.

Keep three failures distinct:

| Failure | Diagnosis and useful repair |
| --- | --- |
| No applicable implementation | Supply the missing body, make an existing body available, or narrow the admitted use explicitly. |
| No unique selected implementation | Resolve the conflict or ambiguity by a stated selection, applicability or intersection rule. |
| One selected implementation returns the wrong meaning | Repair its semantic rule and dependent uses; availability and ordinary types have not established correctness. |

Malformed input, an unbound variable and a language-defined arithmetic error are errors of the represented language or its inputs. A loaded method that is not visible to the running computation is a binding or visibility issue. Diagnose those conditions separately from a missing semantic implementation.

The historical *expression problem* asks for stronger properties than practical plug-in loading alone, including static type safety and extension without recompiling existing code. [Wadler's formulation](https://homepages.inf.ed.ac.uk/wadler/papers/expression/expression.txt) supplies those comparison criteria. Use the name as a search cue; state which properties the actual construction achieves.

#### CMP.15:4.6 - Establish preservation on the promised old uses

Preserve the old meanings as well as the old files. For each established operation, compare which body an old input selects after extension and which dependencies that body invokes. A new, more specific method can redirect an old call in a subtype-based dispatcher. Disallow that override, explicitly retain the earlier selection, or treat it as a behavior change requiring its own correspondence.

For a pure tree interpreter with exact keys, a useful preservation argument is available. Suppose the old keys still select the same bodies, the old expressions contain only old constructors, and primitives, environments and dependent operations retain their meaning. A leaf obtains the same result. At a compound old node, induction gives the same child results, and the unchanged body combines them in the same way. Every finite old expression therefore retains its result. This argument depends on those premises; unchanged source text alone does not prove them.

Test a new form beneath an old constructor as a different obligation. It was not an old expression, so the preservation argument does not establish its new meaning. This case checks whether open recursion reaches the supplied intersection and whether the resulting composition obeys the new rules.

When effects, failures or concurrent replacement matter, use the observations and correspondence from CMP.12 and the interaction method in CMP.14. Preserving a returned number may leave an extra effect or a changed failure observable. Selected tests can expose such differences; a promise for an entire class of executions needs an argument at that scope.

#### CMP.15:4.7 - Bound the cost and retain the simplest adequate composition

Count the work that the architecture moves as well as the work it removes. Independent authors avoid editing a central list, but someone still writes or derives the required intersections, connects dependencies, diagnoses rejected compositions and supports the result. A generic derivation can reduce the number of bodies; its applicability and exception handling still have a cost.

For an exact-key table with `H` supplied bodies and `Q` required pairs, assembly and coverage checking take expected order `H + Q` dictionary operations and order `H` table storage. Each recursive dispatch adds an expected constant-time lookup under the hash-table assumptions. Count the bodies separately: free-variable analysis copies or unions sets, and evaluation may copy environments. With `N` visited nodes and at most `K` names in intermediate sets, straightforward set operations can cost order `N K`, rather than merely `N`. Large-integer arithmetic and representation conversion have their own costs.

A static representation can move selection into compilation or construct terms through operation dictionaries, but it can introduce interface complexity, generated instances, code size, specialization and build dependencies. A dynamic representation adds assembly, visibility, possible runtime failures and often indirect calls. Measure or derive the relevant total for the actual workload; neither label guarantees the cheaper execution.

Compare a closed alternative using the same required cases. For four stable variants, two fixed operations and one maintainer, two exhaustive functions may be easier to understand and maintain than a registry and its coverage description. They still need the correct `Let` rule. Conversely, repeatedly editing another team's module for each new operation or variant gives independent composition a concrete benefit. Use SYSE.23 when the broader engineering choice needs comparison of anticipated changes and their complete cost.

Stop with the smallest construction that provides the receiving application's operations under its admitted inputs and extension conditions. Retain explicit unsupported cases rather than implying a complete open world. Reopen the selection when a new required pair, operation dependency, binding rule, loading condition or change workload invalidates it.

### CMP.15:5 - Archetypal Grounding

#### CMP.15:5.1 - Find the absent intersection before connecting it

Start with integer expressions `Literal`, `Variable` and `Add`, together with evaluation. Contributor A adds nonrecursive lexical `Let` and its evaluation. Contributor B independently adds free-variable analysis for the original forms.

| Variant | Evaluation after A's extension | Free-variable analysis after B's extension |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Literal | Return its integer. | Return the empty set. |
| Variable | Look up its name in the incoming environment. | Return its name as a singleton set. |
| Add | Evaluate both children and add their values. | Union the children's free-name sets. |
| Let | Evaluate the value in the incoming environment, then the body with one local binding. | Not yet supplied. |

If the application accepts all four variants for both operations, seven available bodies leave one required pair absent. The joining contributor derives the eighth body as in CMP.15:4.3. For `let x = 2 in x + y`, evaluation under `y = 4` is 6 and free-variable analysis is `{y}`.

Changing the question to evaluation alone makes the seven-body composition sufficient for that operation. This is a legitimate narrower use, not a repair of the still-unsupported analysis. Changing the binding to recursive `Let` reopens both its evaluation and free-variable rule.

#### CMP.15:5.2 - Assemble and run the contributions with exact keys

The following Python 3 example is a complete small realization for finite, well-formed expression trees. Tuple tags stand for already parsed constructors. It has no parser, effects, method replacement or static type checking. Environments are maps from names to integers; missing names raise `UnboundName`. Set-valued results are compared by membership.

Each contribution is a sequence of explicit bodies. The assembler copies them into a private table, rejects repeated keys and checks any declared required pairs before invoking a handler.

```python
class MissingCase(Exception):
    pass

class MissingCoverage(Exception):
    pass

class ConflictingCase(Exception):
    pass

class UnboundName(Exception):
    pass

def lookup(environment, name):
    if name not in environment:
        raise UnboundName(name)
    return environment[name]

def compose(*contributions, required=()):
    bodies = {}
    for contribution in contributions:
        for operation, variant, body in contribution:
            key = (operation, variant)
            if key in bodies:
                raise ConflictingCase(key)
            bodies[key] = body
    missing = set(required) - bodies.keys()
    if missing:
        raise MissingCoverage(frozenset(missing))

    def run(operation, expression, environment=None):
        key = (operation, expression[0])
        if key not in bodies:
            raise MissingCase(key)
        context = {} if environment is None else environment
        return bodies[key](run, expression, context)
    return run

base = [
    ("eval", "lit", lambda r, e, env: e[1]),
    ("eval", "var", lambda r, e, env: lookup(env, e[1])),
    ("eval", "add",
     lambda r, e, env: r("eval", e[1], env) + r("eval", e[2], env)),
]
data_extension = [
    ("eval", "let",
     lambda r, e, env:
         r("eval", e[3], {**env, e[1]: r("eval", e[2], env)})),
]
operation_extension = [
    ("free", "lit", lambda r, e, env: set()),
    ("free", "var", lambda r, e, env: {e[1]}),
    ("free", "add",
     lambda r, e, env: r("free", e[1]) | r("free", e[2])),
]
joining_contribution = [
    ("free", "let",
     lambda r, e, env: r("free", e[2]) | (r("free", e[3]) - {e[1]})),
]
wrong_join = [
    ("free", "let",
     lambda r, e, env: r("free", e[2]) | r("free", e[3])),
]

old = ("add", ("lit", 2), ("var", "x"))
term = ("let", "x", ("lit", 2),
        ("add", ("var", "x"), ("var", "y")))
required = {
    (operation, variant)
    for operation in ("eval", "free")
    for variant in ("lit", "var", "add", "let")
}

baseline = compose(base)
partial = compose(base, data_extension, operation_extension)
assert baseline("eval", old, {"x": 3}) == 5
assert partial("eval", term, {"y": 4}) == 6

try:
    partial("free", term)
except MissingCase as error:
    assert error.args[0] == ("free", "let")
else:
    raise AssertionError("The absent body was not reported.")

try:
    compose(base, data_extension, operation_extension, required=required)
except MissingCoverage as error:
    assert error.args[0] == frozenset({("free", "let")})
else:
    raise AssertionError("Coverage checking admitted an absent pair.")

incorrect = compose(base, data_extension, operation_extension,
                    wrong_join, required=required)
assert incorrect("free", term) == {"x", "y"}

complete = compose(base, data_extension, operation_extension,
                   joining_contribution, required=required)
assert complete("free", term) == {"y"}
assert complete("eval", term, {"y": 4}) == 6
assert complete("eval", old, {"x": 3}) == baseline("eval", old, {"x": 3})

embedded = ("add", term, ("var", "x"))
assert complete("eval", embedded, {"x": 10, "y": 4}) == 16
assert complete("free", embedded) == {"x", "y"}

outer_name = ("let", "x",
              ("add", ("var", "x"), ("lit", 1)),
              ("add", ("var", "x"), ("var", "y")))
assert complete("eval", outer_name, {"x": 10, "y": 4}) == 15
assert complete("free", outer_name) == {"x", "y"}

shadowed = ("let", "x", ("lit", 2),
            ("let", "x", ("add", ("var", "x"), ("lit", 1)),
             ("add", ("var", "x"), ("var", "y"))))
assert complete("eval", shadowed, {"y": 4}) == 7
assert complete("free", shadowed) == {"y"}

try:
    compose(base, data_extension, operation_extension,
            joining_contribution, wrong_join, required=required)
except ConflictingCase as error:
    assert error.args[0] == ("free", "let")
else:
    raise AssertionError("Two bodies for one pair were accepted.")
```

The absent pair can be found at use or, when `required` is supplied, during assembly. The wrong join passes coverage and returns a set, yet fails the semantic requirement. Supplying both joins fails before any handler runs. These are three different outcomes.

An operation can also depend on another operation rather than only on its own recursive calls. Suppose `IsClosed(e)` asks whether `FreeVariables(e)` is empty. For each admitted variant, its body calls the assembled free-variable operation: `lambda r, e, env: not r("free", e)`. The required set for this use contains both `IsClosed` and `FreeVariables` on all four reachable variants; evaluation is unnecessary. Supplying every `IsClosed` body without `FreeVariables(Let)` must therefore fail coverage before execution. This dependency closure is chosen from the bodies' calls; the assembler does not infer it.

For `let x = 2 in x`, the correct free-variable join returns the empty set, so `IsClosed` returns true. The wrong union returns `{x}`, so `IsClosed` returns false even though all required bodies are present. Both the missing dependency and the wrong meaning propagate into the receiving operation. Calling a private older analysis would evade the selected join instead of repairing either failure.

The `embedded` case sends a new `Let` through an unchanged `Add` body. Its sibling variable `x` still reads the outer value 10 because the `Let` handler extends a copy of its incoming environment. The `outer_name` and `shadowed` cases distinguish the binding rules: the value expression sees the incoming binding, while the body sees the new one.

For this grammar, all recursive calls stay within the declared eight pairs. Coverage checking therefore settles absence for these two operations over well-formed trees of the four constructors. It establishes neither the meaning of a body nor static type safety. Arbitrary supplied Python functions could mutate external state or call other operations; those would need an enlarged dependency account and preservation conditions. The induction in CMP.15:4.6, rather than the finite assertions alone, explains preservation for all old trees under the stated pure semantics.

#### CMP.15:5.3 - Express the same obligation through a typed signature

A static alternative represents a term by its use of constructor operations. Instead of first constructing a stored tree and then dispatching on it, the term receives an algebra: a collection of constructor functions whose common result type `R` is chosen by the interpretation.

The notation below is typed pseudocode. `Base<R>` and `LetPart<R>` are records of functions; `&` requires both sets of fields. It specifies the constraints a realization must enforce, not a claim about compilation by a particular compiler.

```text
Base<R> = {
    literal: Integer -> R,
    variable: Name -> R,
    add: (R, R) -> R
}
LetPart<R> = {
    let_: (Name, R, R) -> R
}

old<R>(a: Base<R>): R =
    a.add(a.literal(2), a.variable("x"))

extended<R>(a: Base<R> & LetPart<R>): R =
    a.let_("x", a.literal(2),
           a.add(a.variable("x"), a.variable("y")))

withLet<R>(base: Base<R>, part: LetPart<R>):
        Base<R> & LetPart<R> =
    {literal = base.literal, variable = base.variable,
     add = base.add, let_ = part.let_}
```

For evaluation, choose `R = Environment -> Integer`. The result of constructing each subexpression is a function awaiting its environment. This delays lookup until the expression's binding context is known. Let `extend(env,n,k)` return a new environment that maps `n` to `k` and otherwise agrees with `env`.

```text
evalBase: Base<Environment -> Integer> = {
    literal = k -> (env -> k),
    variable = n -> (env -> lookup(env,n)),
    add = (f,g) -> (env -> f(env) + g(env))
}
evalLet: LetPart<Environment -> Integer> = {
    let_ = (n,v,b) -> (env -> b(extend(env,n,v(env))))
}
```

For free-variable analysis, choose `R = Set<Name>`:

```text
freeBase: Base<Set<Name>> = {
    literal = k -> {},
    variable = n -> {n},
    add = (a,b) -> a union b
}
freeLet: LetPart<Set<Name>> = {
    let_ = (n,v,b) -> v union (b minus {n})
}

old(freeBase) = {"x"}
extended(withLet(freeBase, freeLet)) = {"y"}
extended(withLet(evalBase, evalLet))({y = 4}) = 6
```

The expression `extended(freeBase)` lacks the required `let_` field and is rejected in a realization that enforces these record constraints. The operation author can keep `freeBase` unchanged; the joining contributor supplies `freeLet`, and the application assembles them with `withLet`. A wrong `freeLet` returning `v union b` has the required type, demonstrating the same semantic limit as the dynamic example.

Here `withLet` copies only the old constructor functions and supplies one new field, so it does not silently override an old field. A richer composition with overlapping signatures needs its own explicit selection rule. Interface union alone does not combine implementations. The chosen language must also support any promised separate compilation; satisfying these mathematical signatures does not establish how a build system handles dependencies.

This representation suits operations expressible through the supplied constructor algebra. Context-sensitive evaluation works because its result is an environment-taking function. An operation needing raw child identity, multiple interacting analyses or cyclic data can need richer results, additional operations or a different representation. Previously serialized trees require a reader that recognizes the extended syntax and applies the right constructor functions; adding `LetPart` does not update an old parser.

#### CMP.15:5.4 - Stop when independent extension has no useful payoff

Suppose a private calculator has the same four constructors and two operations, and one maintainer changes them together. A closed tagged data type with an exhaustive evaluation function and an exhaustive free-variable function makes every required case visible. Adding `Let` means editing those two functions, deriving exactly the same binding rule and checking the new cases.

That arrangement loses independent addition without edits, but the application does not require it. A registry, separate contribution interfaces and loading rules would add work without removing an actual obstacle. Keep the closed design.

If a separately maintained analyzer must later add an operation while another team extends the expression language, repeat the comparison. The new independent change requirement can justify interfaces and an external joining module. It still leaves that module's semantic body to be supplied.

### CMP.15:6 - Bias-Annotation

The worked construction favors explicit finite syntax and pure operations because their dispatch and preservation can be inspected directly. Opaque foreign data, cyclic structures, effects and live method replacement need additional representation or interaction arguments. Do not transfer the tree induction to them solely because their implementation also uses handlers.

The method also makes integration work visible. Contributors who each test only their own extension can underestimate the cost of intersections that appear only in the receiving application. Conversely, anticipated openness can be overvalued when stable requirements make a closed representation adequate.

### CMP.15:7 - Conformance Checklist

- The data variants, operation meanings and admitted receiving uses determine the required combinations, including nested forms and dependent operations.
- Every required new intersection has an obtainable body or an explicit unsupported-use boundary; its supplier understands both sides.
- Generic derivation is justified by the operation's meaning, with binding, control or identity distinctions retained where material.
- The composition defines selection, reports missing support and rejects or resolves conflicts without accidental loading-order semantics.
- Recursive and dependent calls reach the implementation selected for the composition.
- Unchanged sources, separate checking and compilation, early coverage and behavior preservation have distinct stated grounds.
- A semantic counterexample can distinguish a present, uniquely selected but wrong body from a correct one.
- Old-use preservation covers the promised observations and assumptions; a new form below an old constructor is exercised separately.
- The full cost is compared with an adequate closed alternative, and a changed required pair or binding condition has a clear return.

### CMP.15:8 - Common Anti-Patterns and How to Avoid Them

| Anti-pattern | Why it fails | Useful correction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Register first, assume the new intersection exists | Neither independent author necessarily supplied the joint case. | Identify and obtain the joining body before qualifying the combination. |
| Fold every child by default | Binding or control can change how child results contribute. | Derive the rule from the constructor and operation meanings. |
| Recurse through the old private evaluator | A new form works at the root but fails under an old constructor. | Route recursive calls through the assembled operation. |
| Let import order select behavior | Deployment changes can silently change meaning. | Reject duplicate keys or make selection explicit. |
| Treat a successful lookup as correctness | A unique body can return a well-typed wrong result. | Use distinguishing semantic cases and a scope-appropriate argument. |
| Equate unchanged files with unchanged behavior | New dispatch rules or dependencies can redirect old calls. | Compare selection and observations on established uses. |
| Promise arbitrary future combinations from today's coverage check | Future variants and operation dependencies were not included. | Qualify the declared set and reassemble when it changes. |
| Buy openness for an unchanged closed problem | The extra interfaces and support have no receiving benefit. | Retain the exhaustive closed construction while it suffices. |

### CMP.15:9 - Consequences

Independent additions can remain useful without edits to their original modules, while the receiving application chooses the combinations it supports. Missing and conflicting combinations become diagnosable at a stated point. Semantic joining work has an explicit location instead of being hidden in a loader or left to each user.

The price is additional interfaces, composition and qualification. Static checking can move some failures earlier; dynamic composition can admit later choices. Neither removes the need to establish the operation's meaning. A closed design remains a valid result when its total change cost is lower for the actual use.

### CMP.15:10 - Architectural Rationale

The two-axis construction separates knowledge that can evolve independently from knowledge that must meet. A variant author knows the new form's structure; an operation author knows the analysis or transformation. Their future intersection becomes implementable when one contribution can use both. Keeping that contribution outside the old modules preserves their original dependency direction without pretending that the new meaning follows automatically.

The receiving composition bounds the promise. Requiring every possible pair would overstate some applications and make useful partial support expensive. Checking only examples would understate applications that admit arbitrary trees. The required set and its recursion dependencies connect those alternatives to the actual input language.

Exact-key dispatch is the simplest realization in the executable example because it makes absence, conflict and preservation easy to inspect. Subtyping and algebraic interfaces can remove other burdens but require their own resolution or typing conditions. The method therefore selects guarantees independently of binding time.

The semantic rule remains necessary under every realization. The wrong free-variable body passes ordinary type, presence and uniqueness checks in both examples. The explicit derivation and binding variations supply what those checks omit. CMP.12 remains the source of interpretation construction; this method organizes independently supplied extensions of that construction. CMP.14 becomes necessary when effects or changing visible methods alter the composed observations.

### CMP.15:11 - SoTA-Echoing

**How can both axes extend while missing capabilities remain visible?** For a language representable through constructor functions, **adapt** object algebras and typed tagless-final interpretation as the static line used in CMP.15:5.3. [Oliveira and Cook, 2012, sections 5 and 7](https://www.cs.utexas.edu/~wcook/Drafts/2012/ecoop2012.pdf), supplies parameterized constructor signatures and explicit combination of implementations; [Kiselyov, sections 2.2–2.3](https://okmij.org/ftp/tagless-final/course/lecture.pdf), exposes the missing interpretation through constraints and treats deserialization separately. A closed data type with exhaustive functions is the serious cheaper alternative when independent changes are unnecessary. The selected construction removes obligatory edits to a central case definition while retaining explicit new bodies. Reconsider it when raw structure access, cyclic data or interface complexity defeats the chosen representation.

**Can later composition retain static guarantees?** **Adapt** the separation of binding time from checking time in modern compositional programming. [Ye, Sun and Oliveira, 2024](https://yzsun.me/files/ICP-paper.pdf), develops operation dependencies and explicitly supplied extensions for imperative analyses. [Sun, Huang and Oliveira, 2025, sections 3.4 and 6.6](https://yzsun.me/files/CPC-paper.pdf), combines dynamic inheritance through merging with static checking and an implementation of separate compilation through interfaces. These are current research alternatives to treating every late-bound registry as the only open design. They motivate the independent guarantees in CMP.15:4.5; their language proofs do not prove arbitrary user operations correct, and the latter paper distinguishes the core formalization from further implementation features. Reopen a concrete realization when tool support, required effects or compilation obligations differ from those the chosen language supplies.

**How should overlapping bodies be resolved?** **Adopt** explicit resolution rather than import-order selection in CMP.15:4.4. The [Julia method documentation](https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/manual/methods/) supplies a practical comparator: incomparable applicable methods need a disambiguating method, and newly defined methods have execution-visibility conditions. The exact-key table deliberately uses the simpler rule of rejecting duplicates. [Xu, Huang and Oliveira, 2025](https://sec-r.github.io/papers/oopsla25apartness.pdf), supplies a serious research alternative to rejecting all overlap: apartness and guarded subtyping permit overlap that remains distinguishable at use. Those mechanisms still require supplied behavior. Compare again when useful compositions are rejected by the simpler rule or when a new method changes an established call.

**How does an independent join become available?** **Adapt** explicit extension modules from the current [Julia package-extension mechanism](https://pkgdocs.julialang.org/v1/creating-packages/#Conditional-loading-of-code-in-packages-(Extensions)) as a dynamic realization of CMP.15:4.2 and CMP.15:4.5: dependency triggers load already authored code. This improves availability; it does not construct a missing semantic intersection. A static application assembly remains a cheaper alternative for a fixed set. The [Rust coherence rules](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/implementations.html#trait-implementation-coherence) supply a limiting comparator: foreign-interface and foreign-type combinations are restricted, so a wrapper, explicit dictionary or owner-supported contribution may be necessary. Reopen the packaging choice when ownership, compatibility or visibility changes. These sources describe mechanisms, not production guarantees for an arbitrary assembled application.

### CMP.15:12 - Relations

- **CMP.12:** use its interpretation rules and correspondence argument when deriving a body or qualifying preserved behavior; return those results to the chosen composition.
- **CMP.14:** use its interaction construction when handlers share state, produce effects or change visibility during execution. Pair coverage alone leaves those observations unresolved.
- **CMP.2 and CMP.10:** supply recursive construction and representation cost analysis when the extension changes decomposition, storage or access.
- **NOT.2, NOT.3 and NOT.4:** supply expression structure, meaning and permitted transformations when a notation is being designed; the computational implementation here consumes those rules.
- **SYSE.23:** compares the engineering value and full cost of changeability when choosing an open architecture.
- **SYSE.27:** supplies the reproducible extension contribution and support arrangement when separately maintained modules are needed; the joining semantics remains the computational work described here.

### CMP.15:End

# Foundational Thinking DPF Suite Architectural Reference

**DocID:** `Foundational` within **FPF Library**.

> Find the mathematical, physical, computational, modeling or notational contribution your question needs, and understand how the contributions work together.

- **Author:** Anatoly Levenchuk, with AI-assisted development and review
- **Date:** 12 October 2026
- **Status:** Eternal alpha. This edition gives working entries through all five member DPFs and FPF, with their methods, conditions and connections.
- **Publication:** [FPF Library repository](https://github.com/ailev/FPF)
- **Suite:** [The composite discipline and its five constituent DPFs (Foundational Thinking DPF Suite)](README.md)
- **Scope:** Mathematical Thinking · Mathematical Modeling · Physical Thinking · Computational Thinking · Notational Engineering

The Suite also helps when the available concepts or methods cannot express a worthwhile question or construct an answer. A useful result may be a new mathematical object, a subject model or explanatory account, an algorithm, or a notation whose operations make further questions and Methods possible. A subject difficulty can lead to a new formal construction; a new construction can reveal a subject question that was previously unavailable. Research designs, observations and subject knowledge supply their own grounds, while the five contributions here construct and connect the means of inquiry. These results can enlarge both the Suite's own repertoire and knowledge used elsewhere in the Library. The same research programme may draw on several frameworks and contribute to several of them.

If you have a mathematical question already, start with [Mathematical Thinking (MATH)](MATHEMATICAL-PRACTICE-DPF.md). If you need to turn a subject question into a mathematical one, start with [Mathematical Modeling (MMP)](MATHEMATICAL-MODELING-PRACTICE-DPF.md). For a physical account, consequence or observation, start with [Physical Thinking (PHY)](PHYSICAL-THINKING-DPF.md). For algorithm construction, interpretation or analysis, start with [Computational Thinking (CMP)](COMPUTATIONAL-THINKING-DPF.md). For expressions whose rules, interpretation or changes need repair, start with [Notational Engineering (NOT)](NOTATIONAL-ENGINEERING-DPF.md). When the difficulty lies between contributions, use the question index below.

The linked patterns describe methods; their results still have to be obtained or supplied for your situation. A small example shows what that use can produce. A missing result can require a specialist contribution or a further method; a reference alone does not supply it.

Section addresses use `Foundational.Reference:n` and nested numbers. They identify sections of this Reference, not patterns. The contents links follow the heading hierarchy; a complete section includes its child sections up to the next heading of the same or a higher level.

## Foundational.Reference:1 - Start with a working question

| Your question | First useful answer | Open next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I can solve familiar equations, but do not know which objects to use here. | State the needed consequence and choose objects by the operations or maps they must support. An observation or subject premise may still need its own inquiry. | [Construct an unfamiliar account](#foundationalreference31---construct-an-unfamiliar-account). |
| Several physical accounts fit what is known. Which difference matters for the work? | Derive their conditional consequences and construct an observation only when distinguishing them changes the next decision. | [Connect physical prediction and observation (PHY — PH-PREDICT-AND-DISTINGUISH - Develop a physical prediction and the test it needs)](PHYSICAL-THINKING-DPF.md#ph-predict-and-distinguish---develop-a-physical-prediction-and-the-test-it-needs). |
| Two ways of working look equivalent. Can I replace one with the other? | Identify what the replacement must preserve. Matching final values can hide a different observation, enabling condition or cost. | [Understand and change a construction](#foundationalreference32---understand-and-change-a-construction). |
| I must act before I know everything. What is worth finding out? | Formulate which information can reach the choice, compare the consequences still possible, and seek only information that can change the decision usefully. | [Choose with incomplete information](#foundationalreference33---choose-with-incomplete-information). |
| The full calculation is too expensive. What may I simplify? | Select the consequence to preserve, derive the contribution removed detail makes, and seek a replacement, approximation or sufficient bound. | [Obtain a result under limits](#foundationalreference34---obtain-a-result-under-limits). |
| A procedure gives a value, but I need a witness, every answer or a different error guarantee. | Reconstruct the required output, retain enough intermediate information and revise only the shortcuts that relied on the old request. | [Construct and change an algorithm](#foundationalreference36---construct-and-change-an-algorithm). |
| A formula, table or diagram is changed. What should its other expressions now say? | Recover the shared references, interpretation and intended edit; retain independent information and expose a loss or conflict. | [Carry meaning through different expressions](#foundationalreference37---carry-meaning-through-different-expressions). |
| A person or AI supplied an answer. Can we use, alter and extend the way it was obtained? | Recover the needed construction and its conditions, try the changed use, and identify the next useful question or missing capability. | [Continue and distribute thinking](#foundationalreference35---continue-and-distribute-thinking). |
| A local process is faster, but its recipient still waits. What should change? | Reconstruct resource occupancy, transfer and admission rules; compute the alternatives and retain the recipient's event boundary. | [Change an operating flow](#foundationalreference38---change-an-operating-flow-without-hiding-its-waiting). |
| A candidate behaves well in its selection trials but fails in the work it must do. What should change? | Connect the candidate to its actual execution and feedback; locate the failed information, representation, trial or changing operation and examine the resulting way in its intended use. | [Develop a way to act from trials](#foundationalreference310---develop-a-way-to-act-from-trials). |
| I can perform a small operation, but its contribution to the wider inquiry is unclear. | Recover the encompassing work, the intermediate result it needs and the conditions the constituent operation must preserve. | [Keep the vertical visible while doing the work](#foundationalreference39---keep-the-vertical-visible-while-doing-the-work). |
| A claim or recommendation seems plausible, but its support or interpretation is uncertain. | Recover the claims and inference, examine the consequential ground, and follow changed premises into the answer. | [Recover, challenge and revise an argument](#foundationalreference311---recover-challenge-and-revise-an-argument). |




## Foundational.Reference:2 - What this Suite connects

Knowing a formula can leave its use unresolved. A mathematically valid calculation can concern the wrong objects. A computation can return a value after the opportunity to act has passed. The Suite develops ways to locate and repair such difficulties while retaining the contributions that still work.

| Contribution | The work it does | What another contribution can use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Mathematical Thinking** | Construct objects and operations; establish consequences; compare and change constructions. | An object with usable maps, an interpreted expression, an argument, a witness, an obstruction or a qualified approximation. |
| **Physical Thinking** | Identify relevant phenomena, preparation, interactions and constraints; develop and challenge an account of what can happen. | Physical premises, possible changes, a distinguishing observation or a limit on realization. |
| **Computational Thinking** | Construct, understand, analyze and transform algorithms within computer science, including their semantics and interaction. | An algorithm, its representation and correctness, progress and resource conditions, or a limit that changes the requested answer or available operations. |
| **Mathematical Modeling** | Formulate how the subject question, supported relations, unknowns and observations enter mathematics. | A mathematical question whose answer has a stated use in the subject, with the conditions and losses of that use. |
| **Notational Engineering** | Develop expressions and interpretation through which participants can recognize and perform the needed operations. | A usable notation, correspondences between representations and the preparation their readers need. |

Section 5 describes the current repertoire. Choose a method by the contribution the working question needs; combining methods adds value when one result supplies what another requires.

**Methodology connects the contributions to ways of working.** A mathematical construction can describe how operations combine. A physical or computational result can make a different working arrangement possible. Core supplies the general requirements, construction and comparison of ways of working; [MMP.21](MATHEMATICAL-MODELING-PRACTICE-DPF.md#mmp21---compare-interacting-operations-through-mathematical-models) and [MMP.22](MATHEMATICAL-MODELING-PRACTICE-DPF.md#mmp22---construct-a-way-of-working-through-mathematical-transformation) develop the mathematical comparison and transformation when those are needed. Together these contributions support changes in observation, action and division of work without making general methodological development a sixth constituent discipline.

There are two connected questions throughout. How is a claim obtained and warranted? How can its obtaining method and result be used, taught, distributed, changed and continued? Mathematical assumptions, physical premises and computational resource claims need their respective grounds. Their interaction makes a useful inquiry possible; none of the three is recovered merely by relabeling the others.

Here *foundational* means helping enter and develop problems across branches of these fields. A method's conditions still matter: a symmetry method needs a relevant transformation, for example. Further theoretical inquiry can itself be a useful continuation. A problem need not have an immediate commercial application to open a consequential new line of work.



### Foundational.Reference:2.1 - Five subjects and equally legitimate entries

The subject of this composite field is the construction, justification and development of mathematical and physical accounts, computational ways of obtaining results, modeling correspondences and operative expressions. Here an *operative expression* is a formula, diagram, table, program, score, gesture or other structured expression with rules for reading or changing it. Such an expression may be read by a person or interpreted by another system; it need not be executable software. A construction can be developed for its own explanatory or theoretical consequence. Physical application, engineering realization and commercial benefit are not universal entry conditions.

The five branches retain their complete declared subjects. Their DPFs describe selected repertoires within those subjects, not complete textbooks for the academic fields their names may suggest.

- **Mathematical Thinking** constructs mathematical objects, operations and representations; develops arguments, witnesses, countermodels and bounds; and changes axioms or conjectures when the question requires it. Its result can be a theorem, a new construction or an impossibility argument. A proof can finish the work without a physical example. A computational search may help obtain a witness, but the mathematical claim retains its own warrant.
- **Mathematical Modeling** constructs and revises a mathematical question that retains the subject distinctions needed by the intended answer. Its subject may be a physical situation, a way of working, a computation or another mathematical construction. Formulation, observation models, inference, reduction, coupling and return to the subject are work in their own right. A model is not complete for a use merely because an equation has a solution, and the DPF does not cover every kind of modeling.
- **Physical Thinking** constructs and challenges an account of interactions, preparation, constraints, scales, evolution and observation. A physical explanation, discriminating observation or limit on possible transformation can be its primary result. Particular material laws and specialist physical knowledge can be supplied from outside the repertoire. Obtaining a numerical prediction is one continuation, not the definition of the branch.
- **Computational Thinking** develops algorithmics within computer science: effective operations, their representations and semantics, correctness and progress, resource demands and interaction. An algorithm, interpreter, lower bound or changed computational representation can be the result. A mathematical definition of an answer does not by itself supply a way to obtain it. This subject is wider than numerical calculation and narrower than all computer science or software engineering.
- **Notational Engineering** constructs and changes conventions for structured expressions: formation and binding, interpretation, transformation, translation, coordinated representations and the operations their readers need to perform. A usable notation or an improved reading and editing procedure can be the primary result. Its subject includes temporal and embodied notation, not only formulas and programs. Designing a score's timing and reference rules does not perform the music; specifying a gesture's frame does not supply the capability to execute the motion. General semiotics, perception and learning remain outside this declared subject.

These are equal entry points, not stages of one mandatory workflow. Their conditions determine which further contribution is needed. A mathematical question may lead to a more suitable representation; a notational ambiguity may lead to an algorithmic or physical question; a failed inference may require another observation rather than more computation. A familiar adequate contribution can be used directly, without opening the other four languages.

### Foundational.Reference:2.2 - Relations that form the field

The discipline parts are the knowledge and reusable practices described by the five DPFs. A list of publications, shared vocabulary or frequent joint use would not establish their composition. The relations here connect what a construction is permitted to mean and do with how a result is obtained and how a failure changes the available knowledge or practice.

| Connected contributions | Knowledge constrains the operation | Results or failures return to the construction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mathematical Thinking and Mathematical Modeling | The mathematical objects, operations and preservation laws limit which formulations and reductions retain the required consequence. The subject correspondence determines which mathematical distinctions matter. | A counterexample or failed answer recovery can expose an invalid reduction; non-identifiability can show that the formulation cannot determine the requested subject answer. MATH.2/.18 and MMP.10/.12/.14 develop these different repairs. |
| Physical Thinking and Mathematical Modeling | Interactions, preparation, conservation or response premises constrain an admissible physical model; the observation procedure constrains what its variables and data can mean. | A failed prediction, unresolved scale interaction or changed physical constraint can require a different physical account, observation or mathematical formulation. PHY's prediction-and-observation construction and MMP.14/.16/.20 retain those returns. |
| Computational Thinking and mathematical construction or modeling | The required mathematical answer and allowed operations constrain correctness; access, representation, interaction and resource limits constrain what can be obtained. | An effective construction can make an existence result usable. A lower bound or unattainable resource demand can instead require another representation, weaker answer or changed formulation. CMP.1/.8/.10/.11 and the answer-under-limits case expose these differences. |
| Notational Engineering and the other four branches | Binding and interpretation determine which object, observation or operation an expression denotes. Mathematical laws, physical measurement meanings and computational semantics constrain permissible transformations. | A changed interpretation can invalidate a rewrite while leaving the mathematical identity intact. Difficult reading or editing can require a different expression, while the intended operation constrains what that redesign must preserve. NOT.2–.7 and CMP.12 supply the relevant constructions. |

These relations persist beyond a single Work occurrence. A proof establishes a transformation condition that later formulations and algorithms can reuse. A physical experiment can change the premises admitted by later models. A notation repair can change how later readers construct or inspect an argument. The field therefore includes the continued development of the contributions and their connections, not just an occasional team in which five specialists happen to participate.

**A notational entry exposes a substantive difference.** In the [formula, graph and table case (NOT — NT-CHANGE-TOGETHER - Carry a changed request through several representations)](NOTATIONAL-ENGINEERING-DPF.md#nt-change-together---carry-a-changed-request-through-several-representations), `q + q + b` and `2*q + b` agree when q denotes one supplied real value. If each occurrence becomes a fresh sensor read, successive readings 4 and 5 with b=1 give `read() + read() + b = 10`, whereas `2*read() + b = 9` using the first reading. The arithmetic law has not failed. NOT.3/.4 must distinguish the new interpretation and transformation conditions; CMP.12 can give the expression an effective interpreter, and the measurement account supplies what one read obtains. Binding one sample once or retaining two observations answers different questions. The returned distinction can change the notation, algorithm or measurement request.

**A mathematical entry need not proceed to physics.** The [two-element selection case](#foundationalreference35---continue-and-distribute-thinking) asks for a deterministic selection that respects renaming and proves the obstruction. That proof is already a mathematical result. Introducing an order or changing the guarantee to equal probabilities changes the construction; it does not repair the original theorem by a better implementation. The later dispatch example shows how the new construction can then alter a way of working without confusing the mathematical and organizational conditions.

**An algorithmic entry can change what mathematics must retain.** In the [answer-under-limits case (CMP — CP-ANSWER-UNDER-LIMITS - Obtain the answer the work needs within available resources)](COMPUTATIONAL-THINKING-DPF.md#cp-answer-under-limits---obtain-the-answer-the-work-needs-within-available-resources), asking for every optimum rather than one optimum changes the permitted pruning and the contents of a shared table. The optimum value may stay the same. The needed witness information and computational representation do not. This is a connection among answer meaning, representation and effective construction; no new physical theory is required to make it part of the field.

The physical prediction and operating-flow cases in Section 3 show further entries. Their calculations illustrate particular connections and retain their own conditions. None of the cases sets a narrower scope for all five branches.

### Foundational.Reference:2.3 - The whole, its continuity and its boundaries

The characteristic obtained through these relations is the ability to construct and revise a jointly interpretable, warranted and obtainable result while keeping its different grounds recoverable. *Result* includes a construction, explanation, proof, algorithm, model or notation, not only a number returned to an application. The appropriate grounds depend on what is claimed: mathematical validity does not establish physical adequacy; a correct algorithm may be too costly; a physical account does not supply a usable expression; and an intelligible expression does not establish the truth of its contents. A pure proof makes no physical-adequacy claim unless one is actually introduced.

This characteristic belongs to the connection. Several individually adequate results can fail to compose because they concern different observations, discard different distinctions or permit incompatible operations. Conversely, a changed contribution need not defeat the whole: its consequences can be followed to the affected model, algorithm, expression or premise while unaffected work remains usable. For example, an oscillator's numerical error can call for another approximation without rejecting its physical law; a measurement that defeats an idealization can require a new physical or modeling premise that more accurate computation cannot provide. The branches supply the distinct constructions and returns.

The field's identity rests on continuing these five kinds of contribution and their constructive relations. New axioms, physical theories, model families, algorithms, notations, media and specialist suppliers can change without changing that identity. They must still let users recover the relevant meanings, warrants, obtaining conditions and consequences of revision. A replacement for a constituent contribution has to do that work in the connected field. Removing the ability to develop models or notation as primary results, or retaining them only as unexamined inputs to calculation, would change the declared whole. So would replacing this subject by all intellectual work or by the realization of engineered systems.

Field membership does not require every branch to contribute to every task. It also does not require one person to master every method, one publication to duplicate every supplier, or each constituent discipline to belong to only one larger field. A particular use establishes a use relation. Membership in another composite discipline would additionally require that discipline's own subject, constituent knowledge and practice, and obtaining relations; a link or folder location cannot establish it.

The same field is compatible with a larger assembly for formal and empirical inquiry. Consider an assembly whose subject is constructing, examining and revising knowledge claims and the means by which they can be expressed and obtained. It combines this complete five-branch field with research design and evidence criticism, and with the specialist investigative practices needed for its questions. Its boundary includes a proof, a revised physical account, a new model, an algorithm or a notation as a research result; it does not require an engineered realization.

This assembly needs Foundational Thinking's connected contribution, not just five independently supplied answers: a changed claim or observation must remain connected to what its expressions mean, what its model retains, what warrants its conclusions and how a result can be obtained. Research design determines which rival accounts an inquiry can distinguish; these formal, physical and computational conditions can show that the proposed design cannot answer its question. Conversely, actual research material can defeat an observation model, physical premise or inference and return the revision to the affected construction. The Research Method Practice contributions to design, operationalization, criticism and revision explain the other side of this connection.

Compatibility preserves the whole described here. All five primary subjects, their constructive relations and the ability to develop each contribution remain available; a particular inquiry need not use all five. The exposed interfaces include interpreted constructions, warrants and limits, model correspondences, obtaining procedures and the consequences of changing them. They preserve the distinction between mathematical validity, physical adequacy, computational obtainability and usable expression. Changes of theory, technique or supplier can preserve the assembly when these meanings and return relations continue. An arrangement that accepts only computed numbers, subordinates every model and notation to physical prediction, or turns research results directly into authority to intervene does not admit this same whole unchanged. This establishes compatibility with the described possible assembly, not an assertion that another established discipline or published Suite already contains it.

A narrower relation is also useful. Computational mechanics can obtain selected mathematical, modeling, physical, computational and notational contributions together with specialist mechanics and experimental practice. Such a profile can return a failure to the contribution it defeats without importing the entire field. That supply relation is not evidence that Foundational Thinking in its full scope is a part of computational mechanics or Engineering.

The boundary also leaves useful neighboring fields distinct. Research Method Practice can supply empirical inquiry; Explanation Design can supply an explanation for a particular recipient; Human Capability Development can supply representative practice and transfer work; general methodological development in Core can change how contributions are obtained. Financial modeling, operations management, music and movement can provide subject questions or use the results. These relations do not absorb the complete supplying or receiving fields into Foundational Thinking. In particular, general argument recovery in Section 3.11 is a Core contribution used here, not a sixth discipline or a claim to cover all reasoning.

## Foundational.Reference:3 - Working combinations

Use a combination where its intermediate results are needed. Enter with a result already available, take an alternative branch when conditions require it, and stop when the question has a usable answer. The short sequences below explain possible uses; the linked pattern bodies supply the methods.

**Finding FPF and DPF bodies.** Open [FPF-Spec.md](../../FPF-Spec.md) or a linked DPF, search for the full PatternID, and read its Problem frame and Solution. A DPF's own Table of Contents links to the bodies and practical entries. For a large file that GitHub cannot display, use View raw or Download raw file and search the downloaded text.



### Foundational.Reference:3.1 - Construct an unfamiliar account

**Recover the question → choose objects and operations → formulate relations → obtain a consequence → interpret it or revise the failed contribution.**

Start with FPF B.5.FM when the mathematical question is missing. [MATH.16](MATHEMATICAL-PRACTICE-DPF.md#math16---choose-a-mathematical-construction-from-its-required-maps-universal-property) chooses a construction from the maps it must support. MATH.1 and MATH.5 can then construct and interpret composable expressions. [MMP.10](MATHEMATICAL-MODELING-PRACTICE-DPF.md#mmp10---construct-and-revise-a-mathematical-constraint-formulation) expresses admissible subject cases; MMP.11 constructs an unknown relation inside supported conditions. Use FPF C.29 to interpret the consequence through the correspondence between the mathematical account and the working situation.

**Small use.** A cart log records two unit movements. Total distance is two both for forward-then-backward and forward-then-forward. If each entry records an actual signed displacement, assign +1 and -1 and use addition for composition: the final displacements are zero and two. MATH.1/.5 supplies that interpretation. If entries record commands and the cart can slip, the same sum answers a command question. Observation or a movement model must supply the relation to achieved position.

That missing physical account changes what can be concluded. [PHY.4](PHYSICAL-THINKING-DPF.md#phy4---constrain-an-unknown-physical-law-by-transforming-the-situation) develops physical grounds for restrictions on an unknown law. These restrictions can still leave a physical relation unresolved; use supported subject knowledge, observation or a collaborator for the needed premise. B.5.MPC connects the physical, mathematical and computational contributions. Stop with the qualified consequence, or with the particular relation still needed.

The [physical connected-use example (PHY — PH-PREDICT-AND-DISTINGUISH - Develop a physical prediction and the test it needs)](PHYSICAL-THINKING-DPF.md#ph-predict-and-distinguish---develop-a-physical-prediction-and-the-test-it-needs) follows an unknown response through a balance, a conditional prediction and a distinguishing observation. It shows when an experiment is unnecessary and which premise to revisit after conditions change.



### Foundational.Reference:3.2 - Understand and change a construction

**Recover the operations → identify the result to preserve → compare their compositions → carry the consequence into the changed work.**

FPF B.5.RC and B.5.RA recover a construction or argument. MATH.1/.5 builds and interprets operation sequences; [MATH.2](MATHEMATICAL-PRACTICE-DPF.md#math2---treat-objects-as-the-same-while-preserving-operations-quotient) tests whether identifying descriptions preserves the required operations and answer. MATH.16 treats functions as objects with evaluation maps.

**Small use.** Let a stored quantity initially be 1. Operation R returns its present value; W doubles the stored quantity. Performing R then W and W then R both leaves 2 stored. The returned reading is respectively 1 and 2. If the next action uses that reading, equivalence based only on final storage loses the difference the action needs.

[FPF C.39.RQ](../../FPF-Spec.md#c39rq---construct-situated-method-requirements) supplies the situated requirements, [FPF A.3.2.DE](../../FPF-Spec.md#a32de---describe-a-method-for-its-intended-use) describes the Method for its intended use, and [FPF B.1.5.CM](../../FPF-Spec.md#b15cm---construct-and-qualify-a-composite-method) distinguishes obtaining Method composition from a proposed account or another working relation. Use FPF C.29 to establish what the mathematical elements and operations represent in that work, and which conclusions the correspondence supports. [FPF A.3.1.CC](../../FPF-Spec.md#a31cc---check-the-coherence-of-a-method-claim) checks the relevant construction or description claim against its basis and returns a contradiction to its owner; it does not construct the replacement method or establish practical worth.

[MATH.17](MATHEMATICAL-PRACTICE-DPF.md#math17---construct-mathematical-spaces-of-operations-and-operations-on-them) constructs transformations of rules and derives the laws their use needs. [MATH.18](MATHEMATICAL-PRACTICE-DPF.md#math18---compare-mathematical-accounts-through-interpretations) compares descriptions through interpretations and recoverable consequences. For example, preserving how operations compose can permit a calculation in the second description; recovering the first answer also needs a return that retains its required distinctions.

[CMP.14](COMPUTATIONAL-THINKING-DPF.md#cmp14---compose-interacting-computations-through-their-required-observations) develops the algorithmic interaction: expose shared state and allowed observations, construct coordination, and retain separate correctness and progress arguments. [CMP.12](COMPUTATIONAL-THINKING-DPF.md#cmp12---construct-an-interpreter-or-a-meaning-preserving-translation) supplies interpretation or translation when executable descriptions change.

[MMP.21](MATHEMATICAL-MODELING-PRACTICE-DPF.md#mmp21---compare-interacting-operations-through-mathematical-models) derives the consequences of proposed arrangements under a mathematical account of the work. [MMP.22](MATHEMATICAL-MODELING-PRACTICE-DPF.md#mmp22---construct-a-way-of-working-through-mathematical-transformation) uses a mathematical transformation to construct a changed working procedure. The [connected mathematical example (MATH — MP-COMBINE-RESULTS - Change a rule so that separately obtained results can be combined)](MATHEMATICAL-PRACTICE-DPF.md#mp-combine-results---change-a-rule-so-that-separately-obtained-results-can-be-combined) develops local summaries for a distributed calculation, then changes those summaries when the recipient asks for another statistic. MMP.21 interprets the derived differences in the arrangement comparison; MMP.22 reconstructs a candidate way of working from the transformed mathematical operations. The mathematical preservation argument supplies one ground for the change; available performers, timing and practical benefit remain working questions.

For a longer construction, use [MATH — MP-COMBINE-RESULTS - Change a rule so that separately obtained results can be combined](MATHEMATICAL-PRACTICE-DPF.md#mp-combine-results---change-a-rule-so-that-separately-obtained-results-can-be-combined). It follows an unreliable aggregation rule through a counterexample, compatible summary, operation on summaries and proof, then reopens retained information when the answer changes. Each contribution supplies a result the next uses.



### Foundational.Reference:3.3 - Choose with incomplete information

**Recover the available information → formulate the allowed choice → compare consequences → act, revise the requirement or obtain a useful missing indication.**

[MMP.8](MATHEMATICAL-MODELING-PRACTICE-DPF.md#mmp8---formulate-information-dependent-choices-mathematically) formulates what may depend on information available at the time of choice. When a probabilistic recording question is needed, MMP.7 derives the record's law. FPF C.16.IR addresses what an observation relation distinguishes, including bounded indications. C.11.DUA compares the value and cost of further inquiry. The MMP Readme's observation-to-action entry connects these contributions with a usable instruction.

**Small use.** One resource must go to one of two requests. A report identifies the request that needs it with probability 0.8 in the first circumstance and 0.7 in the second. Following the report meets a requirement of at least 0.65 success in either circumstance, provided the report arrives before allocation. A zero-failure requirement remains unmet. If the first circumstance instead has probability 0.95 and the criterion is average success, always choosing it gives 0.95, while following the report gives 0.795.

The criterion, information and timing determine the next move. The mathematical comparison does not require further evidence when those inputs are already sufficient for the intended decision. A statistical fit is only one way to resolve an unknown. If unresolved alternatives all permit the same action, a bound may suffice. Observational agreement also leaves an intervention question open when it depends on an unestablished mechanism.

[MMP.12](MATHEMATICAL-MODELING-PRACTICE-DPF.md#mmp12---formulate-an-inverse-problem-and-choose-whether-and-how-to-use-regularization) formulates recovery from records and makes any added restriction or penalty explicit. [MMP.13](MATHEMATICAL-MODELING-PRACTICE-DPF.md#mmp13---infer-unknowns-statistically-under-a-stated-observation-model) constructs an inferential conclusion and propagates its uncertainty to the requested quantity. [MMP.14](MATHEMATICAL-MODELING-PRACTICE-DPF.md#mmp14---find-and-repair-a-mathematical-models-failed-predictions) constructs a comparison for a consequential discrepancy, revises the implicated component and recalculates the receiving prediction. Use these contributions where the existing law or bound leaves that work unresolved.

[MMP.15](MATHEMATICAL-MODELING-PRACTICE-DPF.md#mmp15---identify-an-intervention-effect-from-available-data) determines which intervention consequence follows from the available data and causal assumptions. [MMP.16](MATHEMATICAL-MODELING-PRACTICE-DPF.md#mmp16---design-observations-to-separate-mathematical-model-alternatives) constructs an obtainable observation that separates a consequential ambiguity and compares its benefit with its burden. [MMP.8.SD](MATHEMATICAL-MODELING-PRACTICE-DPF.md#mmp8sd---construct-a-sequential-decision-model-from-information-and-consequences) retains the information and change law needed for continuing choices.

For a question about the same observed case under another action, [MMP.19](MATHEMATICAL-MODELING-PRACTICE-DPF.md#mmp19---construct-and-bound-a-mathematical-counterfactual-comparison-under-a-causal-model) connects factual inference with changed mechanisms through common underlying conditions. It constructs a joint or nested comparison, or bounds what remains ambiguous. An expected-outcome choice can still be settled by the intervention distributions alone.

The [intervention-and-information example (MMP — MMP-INTERVENTION-AND-INFORMATION - Decide whether an observation will improve the next action)](MATHEMATICAL-MODELING-PRACTICE-DPF.md#mmp-intervention-and-information---decide-whether-an-observation-will-improve-the-next-action) connects these methods: use the supported intervention losses, derive the possible reports, choose whether to observe, and make the later action depend on the received report. If the report no longer distinguishes the possibilities, the observation ceases to justify its cost.



### Foundational.Reference:3.4 - Obtain a result under limits

**State the consequence to retain → derive what removed detail contributes → obtain a replacement or bound → interpret the result at its supported reach.**

[MMP.9](MATHEMATICAL-MODELING-PRACTICE-DPF.md#mmp9---derive-a-reduced-mathematical-model-of-state-evolution) develops this operation for evolution laws. FPF C.29.2 connects a question with an obtaining process; C.29.3 connects that process to physical means. Use the MMP Readme's reduction entry when the removed detail is the difficulty.

**Small use.** Suppose two nonnegative populations satisfy x'=-x and y'=-2y, with x(0)+y(0)=1. Retain only z=x+y. Its derivative is -x-2y, which z alone does not determine: at z=1 it can be -1 or -2. Yet the source laws give e^(-2t) ≤ z(t) ≤ e^(-t) for t≥0. At t=3 the upper bound is below 0.05. A question asking whether the remaining total is below 0.1 is settled without recovering the initial split. At t=1, a changed threshold of 0.2 lies between the two bounds, so deciding whether the total is below that threshold requires more about the initial split.

A smaller model can therefore be sufficient for one decision while lacking a complete evolution law in the retained quantity. New interventions or a different time horizon can require the missing distinction again. FPF's ordinary comparison and improvement methods can retain several complementary models.

[MATH.20](MATHEMATICAL-PRACTICE-DPF.md#math20---bound-a-mathematical-unknown-by-comparable-constructions) now supplies the general bounding method: derive a comparison covering all admitted cases, carry it through the needed operation, and tighten it only if the answer needs more. [MATH.21](MATHEMATICAL-PRACTICE-DPF.md#math21---construct-an-object-through-convergent-approximations) constructs limits and justifies the operations performed on them. Physical Thinking supplies [PHY.3](PHYSICAL-THINKING-DPF.md#phy3---derive-a-physical-limit-from-permitted-transformations) for limits derived from permitted physical transformations, and [PHY.5](PHYSICAL-THINKING-DPF.md#phy5---choose-an-effective-physical-description-by-scales-and-couplings) for choosing which effects must be retained. [CMP.8](COMPUTATIONAL-THINKING-DPF.md#cmp8---construct-an-approximate-computation-with-controlled-error) constructs an effective approximation and finite return condition; [CMP.9](COMPUTATIONAL-THINKING-DPF.md#cmp9---construct-a-randomized-estimator-or-sampling-procedure) constructs sampling and estimation. Numerical procedures are one application of these algorithmic methods. [MMP.17](MATHEMATICAL-MODELING-PRACTICE-DPF.md#mmp17---construct-a-surrogate-for-selected-model-responses) constructs a cheaper supplier of the responses the receiving operation needs. [MMP.18](MATHEMATICAL-MODELING-PRACTICE-DPF.md#mmp18---couple-models-with-compatible-exchanges-and-scales) combines models through compatible exchanges and joint assumptions, retaining consequential approximation and dependence.

The [replacement-and-coupling example (MMP — MMP-REPLACE-AND-COUPLE - Use cheaper models without losing the combined answer)](MATHEMATICAL-MODELING-PRACTICE-DPF.md#mmp-replace-and-couple---use-cheaper-models-without-losing-the-combined-answer) sums two distinct amounts with their error bounds. A tighter decision threshold makes one coarse response insufficient; replacing that response can settle the decision without refining the other model. Asking when the threshold was crossed requires temporal information that the final amounts do not contain.

The full [MMP-SUFFICIENT-ANSWER example (MMP — MMP-SUFFICIENT-ANSWER - Answer the working question before reconstructing every detail)](MATHEMATICAL-MODELING-PRACTICE-DPF.md#mmp-sufficient-answer---answer-the-working-question-before-reconstructing-every-detail) works this connection across MMP, MATH and FPF. Its changed-time question derives the particular initial-state distinction worth recovering.



### Foundational.Reference:3.5 - Continue and distribute thinking

**Expose the missing contribution → recover or obtain the method → use it under changed conditions → choose a worthwhile next question → retain the way of obtaining and using the result.**

FPF B.5.RC/RA recovers the needed construction or argument, B.5.RR follows changed premises, and B.5.QD develops a further question. C.40.CD connects developing problems with developing ways to address them; C.36.RP addresses retaining and renewing methods. MATH.19 constructs a missing argument, MATH.22 follows a change of axioms through its consequences, and MATH.23 develops a next conjecture from a changed construction. [MATH.4](MATHEMATICAL-PRACTICE-DPF.md#math4---construct-a-witness-by-induction) constructs a witness by induction; [MATH.12](MATHEMATICAL-PRACTICE-DPF.md#math12---extract-a-construction-from-a-proof) extracts a construction from a proof.

**Small use.** Ask for a rule that selects one member of an unordered two-element set and respects renaming. Swapping the elements leaves the set unchanged but moves either possible selection. Such a rule is impossible. MATH.13/.9 exposes the obstruction. Adding a distinguished member permits a choice; returning both members changes the requested answer. A program that takes the first stored element uses an ordering that the original question did not provide.

This obstruction opens useful next questions: may the representation introduce an order, does the intended work permit that extra structure, or does it need the whole set instead? A mathematical, computational and methodological discussion can now concern the same identified difference.

**Make the next contribution obtainable.** First locate what prevents its use: an unavailable input, an unexplained relation, an operation the recipient cannot yet perform, or a contributor they cannot reach. C.36.RP distinguishes these repairs. [FPF C.40.PC](../../FPF-Spec.md#c40pc---construct-a-worthwhile-problem-and-proposed-contribution) formulates what a development opportunity could supply; [FPF C.40.DC](../../FPF-Spec.md#c40dc---construct-directions-with-support-configurations) constructs prospective ways to obtain it, including help, access, learning and changed work, with the support each requires. Use an adequate existing arrangement when it already supplies the contribution.

For an explanation, [EXD.1](../EXPLANATION-DESIGN-PRINCIPLES-FRAMEWORK.md#exd1---establish-and-revise-what-a-recipient-needs-explained) identifies the relation this recipient needs. [NOT.3](NOTATIONAL-ENGINEERING-DPF.md#not3---give-expressions-an-operative-interpretation) supplies the reading procedure; NOT.7 can repair an expression that makes the operation difficult. When a human needs practice in using the relation, [HCD.6](../Human%20Capability%20Engineering%20DPF%20Suite/HUMAN-CAPABILITY-DEVELOPMENT-PRINCIPLES-FRAMEWORK.md#hcd6---design-representative-practice-tasks) constructs a task from the later work and its permitted help. [EXD.5](../EXPLANATION-DESIGN-PRINCIPLES-FRAMEWORK.md#exd5---guide-a-recipients-own-explanation) can guide the person's explanation and a revealing retry. Use the response to decide what help is still needed. Reading a worked answer supplies no observation of that person's learning. If later work requires retention or transfer, test performance in those conditions. Use the appropriate training or configuration method when an AI contributor needs a new capability.

**Connected use: develop a selection method that a team can change.** The following is a constructed design example, not an observed training result. A dispatcher must choose one of two equally eligible requests. Their identifiers are arbitrary: exchanging the identifiers must exchange which request a deterministic rule selects, while changing nothing else. The two-element obstruction above shows why those conditions cannot all hold. Choosing the first identifier introduces an ordering the requirement did not authorize. B.5.RA and MATH.13 recover the reason; EXD.1 makes that missing relation the explanation's target.

The team now has a consequential choice. It can supply a meaningful priority, request both items, or change the requirement to equal *probabilities* of selection. These changes answer different questions. Suppose the receiver permits the last option. [MATH.23](MATHEMATICAL-PRACTICE-DPF.md#math23---develop-a-conjecture-by-changing-a-construction) develops the changed claim: a uniform distribution on a finite eligible set is preserved by renaming, because renaming permutes equal probabilities. For two requests, an available unbiased random bit assigns probability one half to each. [CMP.9](COMPUTATIONAL-THINKING-DPF.md#cmp9---construct-a-randomized-estimator-or-sampling-procedure) supplies the construction and its randomness conditions. A temporary ordering can map the two bit values to the two requests; the distribution remains uniform after renaming even though a particular bit value need not select the corresponding renamed request. The resulting guarantee concerns the distribution.

This result permits a division of work. One contributor can establish the selection law, another obtain and implement the random choice, and the receiving dispatcher decide whether probability-based fairness serves the work. People, AI and tools may provide these contributions in different combinations. [MMP.21](MATHEMATICAL-MODELING-PRACTICE-DPF.md#mmp21---compare-interacting-operations-through-mathematical-models) and [MMP.22](MATHEMATICAL-MODELING-PRACTICE-DPF.md#mmp22---construct-a-way-of-working-through-mathematical-transformation) connect the mathematical account to a changed working arrangement: the selected request has to reach the performer, and the permitted source of randomness has to be available. Choose which derivations each contributor needs for their part; the receiver must understand which guarantee the arrangement supplies.

If a human dispatcher can run the routine but says that one unlucky choice disproves equal probability, the explanation has a specific target. Show the two equally likely bit outcomes and their respective requests; ask which outcomes are possible under equal probabilities and what one selection can establish. For practice, change the condition to an available bit that returns 1 three quarters of the time. Directly mapping its values to the requests no longer gives equal selection probabilities. The learner can identify the failed assumption and return the need for another random-choice construction; they need not invent a randomness extractor to make that useful return. HCD.6 and EXD.5 supply the practice and assistance choices. An actual response would support a conclusion about that attempt under its stated help, not a claim of general competence.

**Changed working arrangement.** Two dispatchers now act simultaneously, and each eligible request may be assigned only once. Independent fair choices select the same request with probability one half: of the four equally likely pairs AA, AB, BA and BB, two repeat a request. The earlier marginal fairness calculation remains true for each dispatcher but does not meet the new joint requirement. [CMP.14](COMPUTATIONAL-THINKING-DPF.md#cmp14---compose-interacting-computations-through-their-required-observations) exposes the shared state and permitted histories. A single allocator can randomly permute the two requests and assign distinct entries, or coordinated dispatchers can use an available indivisible claim-and-remove operation. For the latter arrangement, a failed claim must lead to the remaining eligible request; its progress also depends on the service and communication conditions. [FPF C.32.MWA.PP](../../FPF-Spec.md#c32mwapp---construct-and-compare-method-performance-and-provision-arrangements) constructs and compares the corresponding performance and provision arrangements, including allocation and support. The mathematical calculation alone does not install that service or give a performer access to it.

The new problem is worth pursuing because its answer enables parallel assignment without duplicate work. C.40.CD connects that receiving need to the changed method; MATH.23 can investigate how the construction extends to larger sets. A first inquiry can compare allowed assignment histories with the two independent choices, before investing in a general implementation. If one dispatcher already meets the work's needs, this branch can remain a future opportunity; continuing research is not a condition for using the current result.

Keep what another contributor will need to renew the method: the chosen fairness meaning, the construction, its randomness and coordination assumptions, and a case exposing the difference between separate and joint guarantees. C.36.RP also retains access to the needed help or executor. This preserves a way to obtain, explain and change the answer. The same sequence can begin with a failed physical interpretation, an unfamiliar proof or a changed notation: recover the consequential relation, obtain the missing contribution, use it in the receiving work, and let the result open a justified next question.
